papers.title: Inferring Sensitive Events in Multi-Mode Cyber-Physical Systems via Scheduling Side Channels
papers.abstract: Many cyber-physical systems (CPS) are multi-mode: they switch between operating modes with different tasksets and timing parameters in response to physical events or user activity. We show that these mode changes create a timing side channel: by altering the interference experienced by co-running tasks, they let an unprivileged co-resident observer infer sensitive events, such as a homeowner's arrival or a vehicle's route, from its own execution timing and, on multicore platforms, its core assignment. Existing schedule-based attacks and defenses miss this channel because they assume single-mode systems or target a specific, known victim task. We present STAMP, a lightweight attack that needs no knowledge of task parameters or scheduling policy, and works whether or not the system exposes its modes. On a ZoneMinder home-security deployment, STAMP identifies the modes with 94.7% accuracy on unseen hardware, using under 0.5% of one core. On ROS 2 AMCL with the Oxford RobotCar dataset, it identifies which of seven route segments a vehicle traversed with 86.0% accuracy on unseen platforms. A schedule-randomization defense lowers detection recall to 0.53, at which setting only 53.9% as many jobs finish on time. At higher noise ($\epsilon=10$), on-time job completion reduces to 14.4%, while introducing new leakage in 14.1% of the tasksets.

papers.title: Fair and Efficient Distributed EV Charging Coordination Using Threshold Cryptography and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Distributed coordination of electric vehicle (EV) charging with the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) keeps EV constraints private but assumes that every participant follows the algorithm. This assumption fails in practice, where a biased operator or a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacker can send inconsistent signals to different EVs, and compromised EVs can deviate from their prescribed updates. We first prove that attacks by such arbitrarily malicious, i.e., Byzantine, participants do not prevent convergence and therefore remain undetected, and derive the most damaging attack in closed form. We then propose a framework that combines a threshold-signed broadcast with upload recomputation, which detects every deviation without false alarms at linear instead of quadratic communication cost. To keep the optimization running, each affected EV recovers locally with a certified, fleet-aware machine learning price forecast, and we prove that the optimization remains convergent with a recovery cost bounded by the shape of the forecast error. Simulation results with real-world load, price, and charging data show that a biased operator raises the annual cost of disadvantaged EVs by 132.7% and lowers that of advantaged EVs by 49.3% without changing the aggregate load, whereas the defense limits all cost changes to 2.6%. An external MITM attacker raises the cost of its victims by 57.6%, the peak load by 5.8%, and the grid cost by 15.8%, whereas the defense keeps them within 1.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3% of benign operation. With up to 70% of the EVs attacked, the recovery converges in at least 97.8% of the runs.

papers.title: From Pen-and-Paper to Machine-Checked Proofs: Lean for System Identification
papers.abstract: Mathematical proofs in scientific papers are often long and intricate, relying on chains of references to earlier results. This makes it difficult for readers and reviewers to verify each and every step. Interactive theorem proving offers a complement: the theorem and its proof are written as code, and every inference is checked by a small, trusted piece of software called the kernel. This paper serves as an introduction to the Lean 4 proof assistant for a system identification and control audience, assuming no prior exposure to formal methods. We first show how a Lean proof is read using two elementary examples: the first on identifiability, the second on set invariance. We then illustrate how Lean can be used to analyse results from the literature, taking as example a classic lemma on the inversion of the noise filter in prediction-error identification (Ljung, 1999, Lemma 3.1). Since in Lean every step must be justified, the formalization brings to light a subtle point: the original claim of that lemma holds almost surely, although not for every realisation, as its statement may suggest. A simple counterexample makes this concrete. Finally, the paper discusses guidelines and perspectives on the use of Lean in system identification research.

papers.title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
papers.abstract: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.

papers.title: Toward Operationalizing Rasmussen in Evolving Software Systems
papers.abstract: Rasmussen's qualitative drift model explains how successive, locally successful adaptations under efficiency pressures can move a system toward unacceptable operation. Brooker and Hochstein applied this perspective conceptually to software operations without specifying a quantitative procedure for observing drift. We take a step in this direction and propose a runtime observer that quantitatively operationalizes the model's observable part for evolving software. The proposed observer is intended to give engineers evidence for pausing or revising adaptation before declared operating limits are crossed. It tracks how activity or resource use is distributed across components and types of work. Measurement history quantifies accumulated change and recent movement toward or away from current limits. Assuming that direction and limits remain unchanged, the proposed observer calculates the first constraint ahead and the amount of further change required to reach it. Measurements remain comparable across supported component changes, while policy revisions are distinguished from changes in execution. Preliminary runtime studies demonstrated these distinctions under annotated software changes and revised retry limits. A separate multivariate exponentially weighted moving average (MEWMA) experiment detected CPU redistribution earlier with log-ratio coordinates than with raw shares, motivating investigation of representation-dependent observation. Further work will ground constraints in service outcomes, investigate runtime-model acquisition, and test whether decisions informed by observed drift reduce violations at acceptable useful-work loss and intervention cost.

papers.title: A Variational Latent Equilibrium for Learning in Neuronal Circuits
papers.abstract: Brains remain unrivaled in their ability to recognize and generate complex spatiotemporal patterns. While AI is able to reproduce some of these capabilities, deep learning algorithms remain largely at odds with our current understanding of brain circuitry and dynamics. This is prominently the case for backpropagation through time (BPTT), the go-to algorithm for learning complex temporal dependencies. In this work we propose a general formalism to approximate BPTT in a controlled, biologically plausible manner. Our approach builds on, unifies and extends several previous approaches to local, time-continuous, phase-free spatiotemporal credit assignment based on principles of energy conservation and extremal action. Our starting point is a prospective energy function of neuronal states, from which we calculate real-time error dynamics for time-continuous neuronal networks. With this, as a first contribution we provide a simple and straightforward derivation of the adjoint method dynamical equations, the time-continuous equivalent to BPTT. Importantly, additional approximations are necessary to avoid unphysical temporal non-localities. One such approximation was recently proposed in Generalized Latent Equilibrium (GLE), but enforcing temporal locality of the backpropagating dynamics induces an error in the gain that becomes problematic when processing complex signals. Thus, our second contribution is to design a learning rule for the backward weights to find a fully local (in space and time) set of equations for neuron and synapse dynamics that corrects for this gain difference. With this inclusion of backward weight learning, our theory provides a rigorous framework for spatiotemporal deep learning in the brain, while simultaneously advancing a blueprint for physical circuits capable of carrying out these computations.

papers.title: OrbitWeaver: LLM Agent Planning with Simulation Feedback for Optically Interconnected Orbital GPU Clusters
papers.abstract: Space-based data-center designs increasingly consider GPU computing formations connected by inter-satellite optical links. With limited neighboring connections, jobs assigned disjoint GPUs can still contend on shared relay paths. Rank placement and communication priorities jointly affect this contention and the readiness of downstream computation. We present OrbitWeaver, an offline large language model (LLM) agent planner that jointly optimizes rank placement and communication order. Guided by communication structure, execution dependencies, and simulation feedback, the agent constructs and refines plans that coordinate shared-link access with computation progress. This coordination reduces contention and dependency blocking, shortening mean job completion time (JCT). Simulation experiments on optically interconnected orbital GPU clusters show that OrbitWeaver reduces aggregate mean JCT by 6.2-33.5% relative to the state-of-the-art baselines CASSINI, Crux, and Symphony. These results demonstrate the value of LLM-guided planning for efficient concurrent computing in orbital GPU clusters.

papers.title: Coordinated Cooling and Compute Management for AI Datacenters
papers.abstract: The AI datacenters are currently being deployed on a large scale to support the training and deployment of power-intensive large-language models (LLMs). Extensive amount of computation and cooling required in datacenters increase concerns about the energy use and carbon emissions of AI datacenters. Although current state-of-the-art has examined the energy efficiency of LLM inference, most prior research focused on optimizing compute-side scheduling without considering thermal objectives or constraints. Since GPU-intensive inference generates substantial heat that can degrade datacenter performance, ignoring thermal effects can increase total energy consumption and reduce the efficiency of LLM serving. To fill this gap, we profile the characteristics of GPU servers under varying cooling and AI jobs, and develop a joint cooling and computing modeling approach for AI datacenters. Built upon such workload and thermal dynamics models, a novel hierarchical control framework is proposed to co-optimize computing and thermal management by identifying the optimal GPU parallelism, frequency (DVFS), and cooling control knobs. Using real Azure inference traces and detailed GPU profiling, our model balances serving latency and thermal constraints in AI datacenters while significantly improving AI datacenters' energy efficiency.

papers.title: Online Switching Control as Learning with Experts
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the problem of online switching control for discrete-time nonlinear systems where a controller is sequentially selected from a finite set of candidates. The goal is to generate an adaptive sequence of controllers to minimize the cumulative cost under unknown disturbances and cost functions. Specifically, we consider a full-information feedback setting where realized disturbance effects and cost functions are available after each selection. Using counterfactual costs computed from historical data, we reduce the online switching control problem to the experts problem with switching costs. Then, we propose an adaptive switching algorithm based on the Hedge algorithm with a switching suppression mechanism. Notably, the proposed algorithm achieves an expected regret of $O(\sqrt{T\log N})$, where $T$ is the time horizon and $N$ is the number of candidate controllers, while ensuring uniform boundedness of the state. This matches the optimal regret order for the standard experts problem.

papers.title: Symbolic Control for Stochastic Systems via Finite Parity Games
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of computing the maximal probability of satisfying an omega-regular specification for stochastic nonlinear systems evolving in discrete time. The problem reduces, after automata-theoretic constructions, to finding the maximal probability of satisfying a parity condition on a (possibly hybrid) state space. While characterizing the exact satisfaction probability is open, we show that a lower bound on this probability can be obtained by (I) computing an under-approximation of the qualitative winning region, i.e., states from which the parity condition can be enforced almost surely, and (II) computing the maximal probability of reaching this qualitative winning region. The heart of our approach is a technique to symbolically compute the under-approximation of the qualitative winning region in step (I) via a finite-state abstraction of the original system as a 2.5-player parity game. Our abstraction procedure uses only the support of the probabilistic evolution; it does not use precise numerical transition probabilities. We prove that the winning set in the abstract 2.5-player game induces an under-approximation of the qualitative winning region in the original synthesis problem, along with a policy to solve it. By combining these contributions with (a) a symbolic fixpoint algorithm to solve 2.5-player games and (b) existing techniques for reachability policy synthesis in stochastic nonlinear systems, we get an abstraction-based algorithm for finding a lower bound on the maximal satisfaction probability. We have implemented the abstraction-based algorithm in Mascot-SDS (Majumdar et al., 2020), where we combined the outlined abstraction step with our recent tool FairSyn. We evaluated our implementation on the nonlinear model of a perturbed bistable switch from the literature. We outperform a recently proposed tool for solving this problem by a large margin.

papers.title: A Theory of Information Architecture for Networked Decisions: Freshness, Locality, and Coordination
papers.abstract: A broader view of a network can help agents coordinate, but collecting that view takes time. When is a fresh local observation more useful than an older view of the whole network, and when should an agent look only partway across it? We study agents that repeatedly minimize a shared quadratic cost in an environment that evolves independently of their actions. An information architecture specifies what each agent observes and how old those observations are. Each agent uses a synchronized neighborhood snapshot, so extending its scope also ages the nearby readings used in the decision. We assume that the optimal action with complete information is affine in the state, and that the conditional mean of the current state equals the old state scaled by a common exponential decay factor. Using the classical Marschak--Radner decomposition, we derive the delay threshold beyond which fresh local information outperforms a complete but older global view. This comparison allows non-Gaussian states and nonlinear decision rules. We then determine how far an agent should look by balancing the benefit of additional observations against their greater age. In a Gaussian spatial model on a line, we derive the optimal observation radius: looking beyond the local node pays only when information travels more than twice the spatial correlation length in one coherence time. The preferred information architecture also depends on the decision being made. On a fixed 64-node ring, increasing only the reach of the decision weights from 0.7 to 6 hops shifts the optimal observation radius from one to five hops.

papers.title: Symbolic-Permutation-Based Direct Sparse Jacobian Assembly for Accelerated Power-Flow Analysis
papers.abstract: The repeated assembly of the sparse Jacobian matrix constitutes a primary computational bottleneck in the Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis. Through an algebraic operator equivariance analysis of the Jacobian matrix, this paper formalizes the reduction process and proposes a direct sparse Jacobian assembly method based on symbolic permutation. By pre-applying the permutation to the admittance matrix during a fast one-time symbolic phase via its sparse prefix-sum property, the runtime bus-type projection overhead and indirect mapping caches are entirely eliminated. Consequently, complex Jacobian differentiation and global matrix assembly fuse into a single operation, yielding a single-pass, branchless algorithm that streams values directly into contiguous memory. The proposed algorithm is implemented in the open-source RustPower solver. Benchmarks on IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241 demonstrate that the proposed assembly is 28.1-37.9 times faster than the MATPOWER-style baseline and 8.9-9.7 times faster than the in-house Sch\"afer-Braun-inspired assembly (V1); on PEGASE 9241, it outperforms optimized traditional C++ assembly routines by 3.72 times in cold construction and 2.59 times across iterations. End-to-end, the iteration-loop solve time with KLU is 1.16-1.97 times faster than the native C++ LightSim2Grid and up to 95.5 times faster than pandapower, while leaving numerical results and convergence behavior unchanged. The method extends directly to general problems where a sparse Jacobian inherits its structure from a static network operator, including transient stability analysis, EMT simulation, and OPF Hessian assembly.

papers.title: Admissibility-Preserving Control for Block Strict-Feedback Systems Under Time-Varying Asymmetric Actuator and State Constraints
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the tracking control of block strict-feedback nonlinear systems subject to time-varying asymmetric actuator and full state constraints. To that end, we develop a time-varying Admissibility-Preserving Control (APC) framework, in which the Admissibility-Preserving Input Realization (APIR) generates the plant input through a dynamic realization. The APIR guarantees input admissibility under the moving actuator set whenever each actuator bound contracts slower than the decay rate of the realization, and a closed-form lower bound on its gain is derived. The state constraints are handled by a logarithmic barrier coordinate at every backstepping step, with widths measured from the virtual control to the moving envelope of the corresponding state. We prove that every state lies inside its envelope, with each virtual control only required to remain inside the envelope of the next state, while the tracking error converges to zero exponentially. Simulations demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed safety-critical control scheme.

papers.title: RAZeR: Representation Aware Zonotope Reduction
papers.abstract: Reachability analysis is a popular technique for verifying the safety of a dynamical system under uncertainty, where the uncertainty is often represented by zonotopes. As the size of the zonotope representation typically grows as the reachability analysis progresses, it must be repeatedly reduced at the cost of additional conservatism. While various methods exist to reduce the size of the representation, combined advantages are not fully leveraged as only a single reduction method is typically used throughout the analysis. In this work, we show how dynamically choosing which method to use can yield significantly tighter results, thereby easing verification. This is realized by introducing a heuristic, derived from model predictive control, that accounts for upcoming propagation of the current zonotope. We argue that order reduction is not merely a post-processing step after propagation but also a pre-processing step that shapes how the zonotope evolves under the system dynamics. We evaluate our approach, RAZeR, on nonlinear benchmarks taken from the ARCH-COMP, where we demonstrate that RAZeR produces tighter zonotopes at a negligible performance overhead.

papers.title: Learning monotone game-theoretic linear MPC
papers.abstract: We propose a method to learn a game-theoretic model predictive control (GT-MPC) law by imitation from input and output data of a running multi-agent system. By interpreting the recorded inputs as the first moves of the equilibria of a game played by the agents, we learn the GT-MPC weights under hard input constraints and soft output constraints, without requiring the agents to reveal their objectives. We also impose that the resulting generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem is strongly monotone, which ensures the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium and, hence, that the learned GT-MPC law is well defined and can be evaluated efficiently online by variational GNE-seeking algorithms for linear-quadratic games. Moreover, strong monotonicity implies that the equilibrium is almost everywhere differentiable with respect to the references and the weights, which enables automatic differentiation for gradient-based optimization. In addition, we promote closed-loop stability of the unconstrained equilibrium feedback by incorporating a penalty that involves a jointly learned quadratic Lyapunov function. Learning a GT-MPC formulation enables us to explain the agents' objectives, reproduce their behavior in simulation in new scenarios, optimize their set-points, design mechanisms, and enforce additional constraints. A numerical example illustrates the approach.

papers.title: Sub-Synchronous Control Interaction Risk of Large Data Center Loads: A Frequency-Scan Assessment with Cross-Model Validation
papers.abstract: Data centers are now one of the fastest-growing loads on the bulk power system, and most of their demand reaches the grid through power converters inside uninterruptible power supplies (UPS). Whether these loads can take part in sub-synchronous control interaction (SSCI), as wind and HVDC converters do, has not been studied extensively. We examine this question with impedance-based frequency scans at the point of common coupling (PCC). Using a detailed proprietary model (INS-ISU), we scan the motor, variable-frequency-drive (VFD), lighting, and UPS-fed information-technology (IT) branches of a representative facility separately. Only the UPS in double-conversion mode shows negative resistance; it covers the whole sub-synchronous band and continues up to about 170 Hz. The other branches, and the UPS in bypass mode, stay passive. We then repeat the scans on three public models from PNNL, TAMU, and NLR. None of them shows negative resistance in bypass mode, while three of the four models do in double-conversion mode. Lowering the load from rated to light load makes the negative resistance deeper, as expected for a constant-power load, so a lightly loaded facility in double-conversion mode is the worst case. Raising the UPS DC-link capacitance pushes the negative resistance into a narrow band around the fundamental. These findings give a basis for screening data centers for SSCI during interconnection studies.

papers.title: Natural Swing-Up of an Underpowered Double Pendulum
papers.abstract: Robots with weak motors must ride their natural dynamics rather than fight them. We swing up a direct-drive planar two-link robot, whose motors deliver only about 6\,\% of its shoulder gravity torque, along its nonlinear normal modes, two-dimensional invariant manifolds consisting of periodic orbits. On a non-strict mode, injecting energy necessarily moves the state off the manifold, so pumping and stabilization compete for the same bounded torque. We split the input torque into a power-neutral steering component and a scalar pumping input, the only component that changes the energy. The allocation then becomes a linear program in two variables: maximize pumping subject to the torque limits and one control-Lyapunov constraint. The constraint uses the model-based rate of the error, so no stabilizing feedback gain is needed. Experiments in hardware show swing-ups along both modes and compare the allocation with summing-and-clipping and with prioritized stabilization.

papers.title: Battery Energy Storage Sizing in PV Ramp-Rate Smoothing using Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learning-Based Controller
papers.abstract: This paper presents a constraint-aware reinforcement learning (CARL) controller for battery energy storage system (BESS) sizing and photovoltaic (PV) ramp-rate smoothing. Rapid PV power fluctuations caused by cloud transitions can introduce operational and stability challenges in power systems. To mitigate these impacts, grid codes impose ramp-rate limits (RRL) on PV power injected to the grid. BESSs can support such grid codes by absorbing or supplying power during rapid variations. However, the extent to which BESSs can reduce PV-induced variability depends on (i) the BESS power and energy capacities; and (ii) the adopted controller. Thus, BESS sizing and controller design are coupled. Conventional moving-average control can increase battery usage due to filter-induced lag, while ramp-rate control is reactive and does not account for the long-term impact of actions on battery state of charge and future ramp events. Optimization-based methods can reduce BESS requirements by anticipating future PV variations, but their performance depends on accurate PV forecasts. To address these limitations, the CARL controller learns a causal state-feedback policy from historical PV data without requiring forecasts during deployment. Ramp-rate, converter-power, and state-of-charge constraints are incorporated into a causal feasibility interval that guarantees feasible actions by definition. A full-horizon input-convex neural network (ICNN)-based optimization is developed as a noncausal benchmark for the minimum achievable BESS requirements. Evaluation using three real-world PV datasets shows that, at a 10\%/min ramp-rate limit, CARL reduces peak BESS power by 8.7--10.4\% and energy capacity by 47.5--62.6\% relative to conventional ramp-rate control while maintaining the grid-codes compliance.

papers.title: Feasibility of Pareto-Improving Damping Control of Forced Oscillations: The Active-Power Case
papers.abstract: Damping control of a forced oscillation may reduce amplitudes at certain locations while increasing them elsewhere. This paper introduces Pareto improvement as a criterion for assessing such control: at least one nodal oscillation amplitude decreases, while none increases across all other nodes. The analysis considers active-power forcing sources and active-power control injections in connected swing networks with positive inertia and damping. Necessary conditions for Pareto improvement feasibility are derived from the normalized nodal responses. It is proven that for every network with a single oscillation source and a single actuator, at least one positive forcing frequency is shown to preclude Pareto improvement, regardless of the amplitude and phase of the control input. A three-node counterexample shows that this limitation does not persist with multiple actuators. PSS/E simulations of a 6-bus benchmark system and a modified IEEE 39-bus system validated the analysis. These findings suggest the value of assessing control effects across the network and further investigating multi-actuator damping control.

papers.title: Orbit-AWARE: From Onboard AI Deployment to Sustainable In-Orbit Intelligence
papers.abstract: The growing role of space computing in time-critical satellite services makes the long-term reliability of onboard artificial intelligence (AI) a mission-level requirement. Model drift can undermine this reliability through critical-observation suppression or noncritical priority flooding, displacing both mission information and evidence for model correction. To address this drift-induced evidence displacement, this article presents Orbit-AWARE, a safeguard-first lifecycle management (LCM) architecture. A comparison of existing approaches motivates cooperative Data, Cognitive, and Trust Planes for continuous monitoring, event-triggered agentic orchestration, and deterministic governance. The architecture retains a model-independent sample stream before degradation is confirmed and coordinates evidence selection and exchange for diagnosis and ground-assisted adaptation. Candidate updates are verified before control over data disposition is restored. In an xBD-based emergency Earth observation (EO) case study, Orbit-AWARE delivers 14.3\% more critical observations and achieves 8.3\% higher sustainable mission utility than the Rule-Based Drift Loop under a common 10\% downlink budget. Finally, we discuss future research directions for extending LCM through task-aware reliability assessment, memory- and tool-enabled onboard agents, and evidence-centric space networking. This work makes evidence availability and recovery authorization explicit design objectives for dependable onboard AI services.

papers.title: Frequency-Security-Aware Real-Time Economic Dispatch with Data Center UPS Flexibility for Inertia and Primary Frequency Response Services
papers.abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy and the rapid growth of AI data centers are introducing significant challenges to power system frequency security. There is an urgent need to identify grid-compatible resources capable of providing fast frequency support. This paper proposes a frequency-security-aware real-time economic dispatch (RTED) model that enables data center (DC) uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems to provide steady-state power balancing, inertia response, and primary frequency response (PFR) services. Specifically, tractable analytical frequency-security constraints are derived and incorporated into the RTED framework through second-order cone programming (SOCP) formulation. The proposed model jointly optimizes energy, reserve, and inertia to minimize system operation cost while preventing under-frequency load shedding (UFLS). Numerical validation on a modified IEEE 39-bus system demonstrates that the proposed RTED model with UPS flexibility can economically support system operation and significantly improve frequency security under active-power deficit disturbances.

papers.title: State-of-Charge Targets for Storage Participation in Two-Settlement Markets: Reliability, Price, and Compensation Impacts
papers.abstract: As energy storage assumes a larger role in electricity systems, market operation must coordinate its use across time to support reliability during periods of system stress. Minimum state-of-charge (SOC) targets provide a means of preserving energy for these periods, but their design shapes reliability, operating efficiency, and storage compensation. This paper evaluates alternative SOC target designs in a California-based day-ahead and real-time electricity market model. The comparison examines targets based on day-ahead schedules or rolling centralized dispatch, enforced at the individual-resource or system level, across seasons, stress conditions, and participant information settings. The results show that retaining more energy does not necessarily reduce load shedding: targets that restrict discharge can limit storage support during shortages. Under critical summer conditions, individual targets derived from rolling centralized dispatch reduce weekly load shedding by approximately 83--84\% relative to operation without targets. Lower RT clearing costs and average prices can coexist with higher storage compensation, reflecting the role of day-ahead positions and real-time deviations in determining settlement outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of coordinating energy retention with timely discharge and network deliverability when designing SOC requirements for storage participation in electricity markets.

papers.title: Graph Neural Network Prediction of Frequency Nadir and RoCoF Under Topology Variations
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of frequency dynamics under varying network topologies is essential for rapid frequency security assessment, whereas repeated electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations are computationally intensive. This paper develops a topology-aware graph neural network with a radial basis function Kolmogorov-Arnold network (RBF-KAN) regression head, termed RK-GNN, to predict frequency nadir and maximum absolute rate of change of frequency (RoCoF). Scenarios combine load scaling, regional load redistribution, and generator redispatch with intact, N-1, and N-2 transmission topologies. After checks for network connectivity, generator reference limits, and numerical consistency, the retained scenarios are simulated in PSCAD to construct the reference dataset. The RK-GNN is evaluated against a conventional deep neural network (DNN) and a baseline GNN. On the IEEE 39-bus system, the RK-GNN reduces the mean absolute errors (MAEs) of nadir and RoCoF by 48% and 59% relative to the DNN and by 42% and 61% relative to the baseline GNN. Incorporating the bridge indicator and disturbance hop distance yields further MAE reductions of 27% and 54%. These results show that the proposed topology-aware architecture provides accurate prediction of both frequency metrics under varying topologies and substantially reduces the need for repeated EMT simulations.

papers.title: Improved Closed-Form Identification of the Air-Gap Permeance in Magnetic Equivalent Circuits of Rotor-Eccentric Electric Motors
papers.abstract: Fast and accurate simulation of electric motors is essential for their design, fault diagnosis and control. Magnetic equivalent circuits (MECs) offer a computationally efficient alternative to the finite element method (FEM), yet their flux tube representation poorly captures the air-gap field. This creates a challenge, as the air gap stores most of the magnetic energy and governs the electromagnetic torque and, in rotor-eccentric motors, the unbalanced magnetic pull (UMP). Existing air-gap permeance expressions vary widely in their results for torque ripple and UMP and account for tooth-normal eccentricity only. This paper proposes the dual-term air-gap permeance (DTAP) model, a closed-form expression for the air-gap permeance between a stator and a rotor tooth that accounts for tooth-normal and tooth-tangential eccentricity, with and without rotor skew. Its parameters are identified from a FEM model of the air gap and the complete set of tooth heads, which includes the shielding by the neighbouring teeth. For three motors, DTAP reproduces the FEM air-gap permeance with a 2.8-4.8 times smaller error than the state of the art, at a comparable computational cost. Implemented in the MEC of an eccentric induction motor, it reproduces the torque ripple within 1.6% and the peak UMP within 1.3% of the reference, i.e., with 2.8 and 27 times smaller deviations than the state of the art. DTAP thereby enables MEC to predict the torque pulsations and bearing loads of eccentric motors more accurately without sacrificing computational speed.

papers.title: Implicit discretization of PID-like sliding-mode control with third-order output accuracy
papers.abstract: A digital PID-like sliding-mode controller is proposed for a double integrator with a Lipschitz matched disturbance. A proper implicit discretization, matched to the exact sampled dynamics of the plant, attains the accuracy of the continuous-time controller without discretization chattering. Global finite-step convergence to a discrete-time sliding mode is established for two gain designs and every sampling time, using an implicit Lyapunov function and a computer-assisted certificate in exact arithmetic. The resulting controller provides third-order output accuracy, second-order accuracy for its derivative, and exact finite-time rejection of constant matched disturbances. These accuracy orders are proved to be optimal among deterministic causal controllers using the same sampled information.

papers.title: PLL-Less Synchronization of Grid-Following Converters Using a Voltage-Driven Frenet Frame
papers.abstract: In grid-following converters, the synchronization path can transmit voltage disturbances to the current loop under weak or unbalanced grid conditions. This paper develops a Frenet-frame controller that derives its axes from the integral curve of the measured voltage at the point of common coupling. The tangential current governs active power, while the normal and binormal currents govern the transverse components of non-active power. Feedforward terms derived from the output filter model compensate curvature and torsion coupling, yielding identical nominal current dynamics across the axes. The controller operates without a phase-locked loop or sequence extraction. A reduced transverse model accounts for the finite bandwidth of geometric rate reconstruction and predicts a reduction in low-frequency coupling from voltage disturbances to current. Controller hardware-in-the-loop tests using real-time simulation of a three-phase four-wire converter show the shortest settling time after an active power reference step and the smallest peak power deviations during balanced voltage disturbances among the tested controllers. Under single-phase voltage unbalance, the method reduces peak binormal current and maximum phase-current total harmonic distortion relative to both benchmarks. It also settles to the commanded power in a weak-grid connection test where the phase-locked loop benchmark exhibits sustained oscillations.

papers.title: Enhancing Transient Stability of VSG-Controlled Converters Under Grid Frequency Disturbances
papers.abstract: Strong damping feedback can substantially improve the transient synchronization stability of renewable energy converters employing virtual synchronous generator (VSG) control. However, conventional damping feedback uses the nominal frequency as its reference. When the frequency of a weak grid deviates from nominal, strong damping tends to keep the VSG frequency near nominal. This can sustain a frequency difference between the VSG and the grid and compromise transient synchronization. To address this problem, this paper proposes a complex-frequency-based method to estimate the grid reference frequency from local terminal measurements. The estimated frequency replaces the nominal reference in the VSG synchronization loop, so that damping acts on the frequency difference between the VSG and the real grid. Controller hardware-in-the-loop tests validate the effectiveness of the proposed method under grid frequency disturbances and its robustness to grid parameter uncertainty and adverse grid conditions.

papers.title: Data-Driven Output Regulation via Predictive Control
papers.abstract: This paper addresses constrained output regulation for unknown linear systems by means of predictive control directly from input-output data. The objective is to reject disturbances and track references generated by a known exosystem, without identifying a plant model or solving the output regulator equations. The first step is a trajectory parametrization for plants driven by exosignals with known dynamics. % By exploiting the known exosystem eigenstructure, Willems et al's fundamental lemma is extended from autonomous input-output trajectories to trajectories coupled with exogenous modes. By exploiting the known exosystem eigenstructure, input-output trajectories driven by an exosignal of known phase are parametrized directly from data, which contains the affine version of Willems et al.'s fundamental lemma as a special case. This parametrization yields a nominal data-driven predictive control (DDPC) regulator, for which a Lyapunov argument proves exponential convergence to the regulator manifold. For periodic exosignals, the steady-state feedforward input is eliminated from the online problem through an incremental-input regularization, leading to an implementable regulator based on measured data and known exosystem information. Bounded output noise is handled by slack and coefficient regularization, with a regularization center computed offline from data; the resulting robust DDPC law is recursively feasible and practically stabilizing, with an ultimate regulation error that vanishes with the noise bound. A constrained lateral vehicle-control example with periodic road curvature illustrates disturbance rejection, input-constraint satisfaction, and the transition from exact regulation with noise-free data to practical regulation with noisy data.

papers.title: Latent resonances in oscillator networks
papers.abstract: In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.

papers.title: Grid-Compliance Testing of Wind Turbines through Virtualized Component Tests: Testing Concept and Test Bench
papers.abstract: As the proportion of inverter-connected wind turbines increases, test methods for evaluating their grid behavior are becoming increasingly important. This paper presents a Power Hardware-in-the-Loop (PHiL)-based method for grid connection testing of wind turbines. For the first time, geographically distributed simulations of aerodynamics via the Internet and of the grid model via a fiber-optic connection are integrated into certification-relevant tests. The concept expands upon the methods described in IEC TS 61400-21-4. Initial experimental results confirm high emulation quality and sufficiently low latencies, and meet the requirements for a standards-compliant grid emulation.
